title: ICC Freezes Cricket Canada's Funding — And a Diaspora Community Holds Its Breath
excerpt: With 63% of its revenue from ICC distributions, Cricket Canada's six-month funding suspension over governance failures threatens grassroots programmes that serve millions of Indo-Canadians
body:
The International Cricket Council has suspended all funding to Cricket Canada for six months, a punishing intervention that strikes at the heart of one of the diaspora's most passionate sporting communities. The decision, announced this week, follows mounting concerns over governance failures, financial irregularities, and an ongoing anti-corruption investigation that has cast a long shadow over Canadian cricket.

A Financial Lifeline, Severed

The numbers tell a stark story. ICC distributions accounted for 63 per cent of Cricket Canada's total revenue in 2024 — making the global body's funding not merely a supplement but the organisation's financial backbone. Without it, Cricket Canada faces an existential squeeze on its administrative operations, development programmes, and the grassroots infrastructure that serves hundreds of thousands of players across the country.

The ICC was careful to note that national team activities, including high-performance programmes, will continue unaffected during the suspension period. But the freeze sends an unmistakable message: governance standards are non-negotiable.

The Corruption Cloud

The funding suspension did not arrive in isolation. Cricket Canada has been mired in controversy since a CBC documentary exposed allegations of corruption within the organisation. A leaked recording allegedly captured former coach Khurram Chohan discussing pressure to select specific players — a claim that triggered an ICC Anti-Corruption Unit investigation into Canada's performance at the 2024 T20 World Cup.

The administrative turmoil extended to the top. Former CEO Salman Khan was removed amid legal issues, and the organisation's board underwent a wholesale restructuring. The new leadership, installed with the promise of reform, has so far been unable to convince the ICC that sufficient progress has been made.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.8 million people of Indian origin living in Canada, cricket is far more than a sport — it is a cultural anchor, a weekend ritual, and increasingly, a pathway for the next generation. Canada's T20 World Cup campaign in 2024, co-hosted on home soil, was a watershed moment that drew massive South Asian crowds and briefly made cricket front-page news in a country where it rarely registers.

The funding freeze threatens to undo that momentum. Local leagues, coaching academies, and talent identification programmes — many of which serve Indo-Canadian communities in the Greater Toronto Area, Vancouver, and Calgary — depend on trickle-down funding from the ICC's distributions.

"Cricket is the one thing that brings our community together on weekends," says a volunteer organiser from a Brampton-area league. "If the national body can't function, everything below it suffers."

The Path Forward

Cricket Canada's new board has signalled its intent to address the governance deficiencies head-on, implementing compliance reforms and cooperating with the ICC's investigations. The six-month timeline offers a clear window: demonstrate meaningful progress, or face the prospect of even harsher sanctions.

The situation also carries implications beyond Canada's borders. The ICC has simultaneously reprimanded USA Cricket for similar governance and financial failures, suggesting a broader reckoning for Associate nations that have struggled to professionalise their administration. For cricket's global ambitions — particularly ahead of the sport's return to the Olympics in 2028 — the health of its North American operations is no longer a peripheral concern.

For NRI cricket fans who have watched the sport grow from backyard tape-ball games to televised T20 spectacles, the message is clear: the institutions that steward that growth must match the community's ambition with accountability.
nri_angle: Cricket Canada's funding crisis directly impacts the 1.8 million Indian-origin Canadians for whom the sport is a cultural anchor — from weekend leagues in Brampton to youth academies in Vancouver.
author: Diaspora Desk
